name: Ivan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Kerr's, which is forty acres of apple orchard, three thousand laying hens in mobile sheds, and hay meadows, with a few pigs to eat the windfalls. Mrs Kerr runs it with her nephew Callum. I start at half six with the hens, collect and grade eggs, move the sheds onto fresh grass, and then it's the orchard: pruning in winter, thinning in summer, picking in autumn. I'm still not a good pruner; Mrs Kerr walks behind me and tuts. But the eggs I'm good at.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Butcher's counter, eighteen years, at Halloran's on the high street. A big supermarket opened on the bypass and in two years the shop was gone. Kerr's needed someone and I was used to early mornings and hard work. My wife Kati works mornings at the bakery, and we've got Dominik, fifteen, and Eszter, eleven. I use the AI on my phone sometimes, to ask about frost or how to treat scab on the apples, but I check with Mrs Kerr before I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and get back to work. A man should earn his living with his hands and his head, not by waiting for a machine. I'd say it at the men's breakfast at church, maybe, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I keep learning and maybe one day I'm good enough at pruning to stop the tutting. I'd like that. And I'd keep saving for what I really want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Put my eighty a month into the savings jar for a smallholding, and do the orchard pruning course Mrs Kerr keeps talking about. Ask Callum to show me how he does the egg orders on the computer, since that's useful anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the smallholding you're saving for.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few acres, my own hens, a couple of pigs, and do a bit of butchery for neighbours, the proper way. Everyone dreams of a boat or a beach. I dream of ten acres and a cold room for hanging pork. Kati laughs at me, but she likes the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supermarkets, still. They killed the butcher's, and they squeeze Mrs Kerr on the egg price now. That's competition, I know. But it's not always fair competition when one side is that big.

S0.say: He'd say good and get back to work, because a man should earn his living with his hands and head. He'd say it at the church men's breakfast, not online.
S0.think: He keeps learning the work and saving for what he really wants, and hopes to improve his pruning.
S0.do: Carries on, putting eighty a month towards a smallholding and taking the orchard pruning course. Asks the farmer's nephew to teach him the computer egg orders.
S0.quote: Everyone dreams of a boat or a beach. I dream of ten acres and a cold room for hanging pork.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan's dream of a small farm with a cold room for hanging pork shapes everything he says. A former butcher whose shop was killed by a supermarket, he accepts competition but thinks very large players aren't always fair. He's an occasional AI user who checks its answers with the farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market changes and you change with it, that's how it's always been. I'd say young people should learn a trade properly, with an apprenticeship, not just learn to press buttons. I wouldn't moan about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, picking is the job they'd come for first. There are already apple-picking robots with little vacuum arms. If Kerr's gets one, my autumns go, and my hours go down. Hens, they'd still need me for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Kerr to keep me on the hens and learn the egg grading machine properly, the new one with the camera. I'd use the AI a bit more for planning, egg orders and feed. And I'd keep saving, but maybe a bit less for the smallholding and more for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not too bad, but the smallholding feels further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dominik say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Dominik's into computers. He'd tell me to stop being stubborn and learn it. He'd probably be right. My son explaining robots to me at the kitchen table, and me nodding like I understand. That's how it'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been through one job ending. Does this feel like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Halloran's closing was worse, because I didn't see it coming. This I'd see coming. That's a big difference for a man with a mortgage.

S1.say: He'd say the market changes and you change with it, and that young people should learn a proper trade through apprenticeships, not just button-pressing. He wouldn't moan.
S1.think: He thinks apple picking would be automated first, cutting his autumn hours, though the hens would still need him for a while.
S1.do: Asks to stay on the hens and learn the camera egg grader properly, and uses AI more for orders and feed planning. Shifts some savings from the smallholding fund to a rainy-day fund.
S1.feel: Uneasy; not too bad, but the smallholding dream feels further away.
S1.quote: My son explaining robots to me at the kitchen table, and me nodding like I understand. That's how it'd go.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan accepts market change in principle and is willing to learn the new kit once it's in front of him. His son is the family's tech guide, which he finds a little funny. Losing the butcher's shop with no warning makes him value seeing this one coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and it's not a fair market when a few companies own everything that works. I don't normally want the government involved, but I'd want them to stop it being a free-for-all. I'd say that at church and probably at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished at Kerr's. Picking, hens, pruning, if a robot can do it all, and Mrs Kerr's struggling for money, she'd have to. And Kati's bakery, if a machine can make the bread, that's her mornings too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First weekend, we'd cut everything: no new phone for Dominik, no holiday, the satellite TV goes. I'd start doing home butchery for people round here, half a pig, a lamb, cash, while folks still want a man they know cutting their meat. And I'd talk to my brother in town about helping each other out, sharing the car, the shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep much. I'd be up at three working sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the smallholding savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smallholding money would go into the mortgage, all of it. Eight years of saving for my ten acres, and it'd go to keep the bank off my front step. That's the bit I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you could sell that a robot can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Butchery, for a while. People round here like to know who cut their meat. But if robots are cheap and good, I don't know for how long. A year? Maybe less.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast and not a fair market when a few companies own everything that works. Unusually for him, he'd want the government to stop it being a free-for-all.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be finished at the orchard farm, and his wife's bakery job could go too if machines make the bread.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, including a phone for his son, the holiday and satellite TV. Starts home butchery for neighbours for cash, shares a car and shopping with his brother, and puts the smallholding savings into the mortgage.
S2.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep and doing sums at three in the morning.
S2.quote: Eight years of saving for my ten acres, and it'd go to keep the bank off my front step.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI makes Ivan, a free-market man, want government rules, which he acknowledged himself. Losing eight years of smallholding savings to the mortgage was the deepest hurt. His fallback is his old butchery trade, sold on trust, though he doubts it would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get your own house in order and not rely on anyone. I'd tell the young lads at church to learn a trade that needs a person in the room. And I'd say the companies should pay for proper apprenticeships, since they're making the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I'd have a chance. I'd be forty-eight. If I build up the butchery on the side now, I might have a name round here by the time it lands, and people pay for a name they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get my food hygiene certificate sorted and turn the old garage into a small cutting room, maybe two thousand to do it properly. I'd do butchery for neighbours at weekends, keep the Kerr's job in the week. Whatever it earns goes half to savings, half back into kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's a working anxious, if that makes sense. I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that a risk, spending money on kit when the end point is the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Kati would say I'm spending money we need on a dream. If the robots are coming anyway, I'd rather lose my money on my own dream than on someone else's mortgage payments. She'd tell me that's not how money works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have tried. I'd still have the tools and the room. My father always said, a man who can feed people won't starve.

S3.say: He'd say five years is time to put your own house in order without relying on anyone, urge young people to learn trades that need a person, and want companies to fund apprenticeships.
S3.think: At 48 he thinks he'd have a chance if he builds up a butchery name locally now, because people pay for a name they trust.
S3.do: Gets a food hygiene certificate and spends about two thousand turning the garage into a small cutting room. Does weekend butchery for neighbours while keeping the farm job, splitting earnings between savings and kit.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a working anxiety that keeps him busy.
S3.quote: If the robots are coming anyway, I'd rather lose my money on my own dream than on someone else's mortgage payments.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Ivan bet on his old trade and his local reputation, and he knows his wife thinks it's risky. His thinking is rooted in self-reliance and trust between neighbours. He accepted the risk calmly, quoting his father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say families should plan together, the young ones learning trades, the old ones passing on what they know. And I'd say it with my sleeves rolled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. Dominik would be twenty-five, Eszter twenty-one. The mortgage would be nearly done. I think I could do it, buy a few acres, run the butchery, keep hens. It's my dream, just with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Kerr's for a few years and keep saving, aiming for a deposit on land by year five or six. I'd build the weekend butchery slowly. And I'd sit down with Dominik about his plans, see if he wants to come in with me or do something else that robots can't, like an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's hope in it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot farming next door worry you, if you had your own few acres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. In a world full of robot food, I think somebody will pay extra for sausages made by a man who knows the pig's name. Maybe I'm a romantic. Kati says I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if nobody pays extra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be a romantic with ten acres, which isn't the worst thing. I'd grow our own food at least. We'd not go hungry.

S4.say: He'd say a decade is plenty for anyone willing to work, and families should plan together, with the young learning trades and the old passing on what they know.
S4.think: At 53, with children grown and the mortgage nearly done, he thinks he could buy a few acres and run the butchery: his dream with a deadline.
S4.do: Stays at the orchard farm for a few years while saving for a land deposit by year five or six. Builds the weekend butchery slowly and talks with his son about joining him or choosing a robot-proof trade.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with hope in it.
S4.quote: In a world full of robot food, I think somebody will pay extra for sausages made by a man who knows the pig's name.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, the threat becomes a deadline for Ivan's long-held dream rather than a reason to give it up. He's betting on people paying more for food from someone they know, and admits he may be a romantic. Self-reliance and family run through his plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's both of us, me and Kati, and my smallholding money goes into the mortgage. What would help is the market staying fair, so small people can still sell to their neighbours, and help with apprenticeships and setting up a small business, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about food. Everyone talks about jobs, but people still have to eat, and they like to know where it's from. When Halloran's closed, old ladies cried at the counter, not because of the meat, because of us.

headlineQuote: When Halloran's closed, old ladies cried at the counter, not because of the meat, because of us.
portrait: Ivan Varga is 43, a newer hand on an orchard and laying hen farm, two years in after eighteen years on a butcher's counter that closed when a supermarket opened. He's traditional, believes in fair markets, trades and apprenticeships, and uses AI now and then but checks it with his boss. He's calm or uneasy in the milder pictures and keeps saving for his dream of a smallholding with a cold room. AGI in 2 years alarms him because his wife's bakery job would go too and the smallholding money would go into the mortgage. With 5 or 10 years he bets on home butchery and a few acres, trusting neighbours to pay for food from someone they know.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he and his wife would both lose work and his smallholding savings would go into the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A fair market where small sellers can still sell to neighbours, plus help with apprenticeships and setting up small businesses rather than handouts.
